$comment: A skill is mostly prompt, which makes it the easiest thing in the world to write badly and never notice. The two stages people skip are the two that matter: what it must NEVER do, and testing that it actually fires when it should.

stages.title: Idea
stages.plain: What the skill does, in one sentence.
stages.ask: What should this skill do? One sentence. If it takes two, it may be two skills.
stages.done: One sentence, and a note of anything nearby that is deliberately a different skill.

stages.title: Triggers
stages.plain: What someone says or does that should make this fire.
stages.ask: What would you have typed, the moment you wanted this? Give real phrasings, including lazy ones.
rules: Collect real phrasings, not canonical ones. Nobody types the canonical one.
Also collect near misses that must NOT fire it. A skill that fires too often gets uninstalled faster than one that never fires.
stages.done: A list of should-fire phrasings and a list of must-not-fire ones.

stages.title: Never do this
stages.plain: The things it must refuse or hand back, before any of it is written.
stages.ask: What should this skill never do on its own? Anything expensive, destructive, or outward-facing?
stages.done: A short list, each with the reason, because a rule with a reason survives a case it did not anticipate.

also_ask.q: I have everything I need. Should I run to the end and bring you the questions at the finish, or stop at each decision?

options.full: Run to the end. Every question waits for the finish.
options.product: Decide the technical things alone. Stop when it changes what someone sees or reads.

also_ask.why: Asked here rather than at setup because this is the moment the person actually knows how much they trust the plan. The setup answer is the default, not the verdict.

stages.title: Research
stages.plain: Codex checks how the host actually loads skills right now.
brief_must_ask: What is the current required structure of a skill for each target host, and where is that documented?
Which frontmatter fields exist today, which are required, and what are the real limits on each?
How is a skill's description used to decide when it fires?
What changed recently enough that a model trained earlier would get it wrong?
stages.done: A briefing with the current file layout and frontmatter contract, each claim sourced.

stages.title: Write it
stages.plain: SKILL.md and any reference files, grounded on the research.
rules: The description is the trigger. Write it for matching, and make it short enough to read in a list.
Instructions state what and why. A rule with a reason adapts to a case it never anticipated; a rule without one breaks on the first unusual input.
Anything long, stable or reference-shaped goes in a separate file, not in SKILL.md.
stages.done: The skill exists and its structure matches what the research established, not what was remembered.

stages.title: Trigger test
stages.plain: Say the real phrasings and check it fires. Say the near misses and check it does not.
stages.done: Every should-fire phrase fires it. Every must-not-fire phrase does not. Failures are fixed in the description, which is where triggering is decided.
rules: Assert the skill file EXISTS before interpreting any match result. A grep against a missing file returns non-zero exactly as a phrase-not-found does, so a probe that maps both to success reports a pass for a skill that was never written. Found by the debate stage doing precisely this.
Report three states, not two: fires, does not fire, and cannot read. Collapsing the third into either of the first two is what makes a green trigger test meaningless.
The description is where triggering is decided, so failures are fixed there rather than in the body.

stages.title: Debate
stages.plain: Both agents review the skill and argue about it once.
stages.done: Every concern is fixed, defended with a reason, or in the final question round.

stages.title: Done
stages.plain: It installs, it fires, it does the thing, and it refuses what it should.
stages.done: Installed from a clean state, triggers verified both ways, one real task completed end to end, guardrails checked.
stages.gate_cmd: test -f SKILL.md && grep -q '^name:' SKILL.md && grep -q '^description:' SKILL.md

gate_cmd_note: A stage is done when its gate_cmd exits zero, not when an agent says so. {{cmd.X}} resolves from commands.* in .duet/config.json, detected once by lib/duet-detect.sh. {{out}} is the phase output path. Human gates carry no command, because 'the human confirmed' is not a command.
